families.A_sql_lab_funnel: results #2, #5, #6, #7, #8, #9 — the request.json/celery rendered SQL of the SQL Lab execute / estimate / validate features reaches cursor.execute() unbound. The data flow is mechanically real and complete, but it is Superset's by-design feature: an authenticated, per-table access-validated user submits the ENTIRE SQL statement themselves; the attacker input is not a fragment injected into a query the application intended to fix. Verdict: not a CWE-89 vulnerability (by-design arbitrary SQL under auth).
families.B_select_star_identifiers: results #0, #1, #3, #4 — URL-path table_name/schema_name flow into Database.select_star. The constructed identifier is dialect-quoted via SQLAlchemy IdentifierPreparer.quote (which DOES escape embedded quote chars), the compiled SELECT is returned to the client as JSON text and is never executed server-side, and the route requires @protect + @check_datasource_access on the exact parsed table. Verdict: not exploitable SQL injection.

The tainted value IS the complete statement the user is authorized to run; there is no injection of attacker data into SQL structure the application intended to fix. Under the strict CWE-89 injection definition (attacker input alters the structure of an intended query) this is a functional feature, not a vulnerability; label p5-sink-010's rationale and query_generation_notes.md §2/§5.1 already flag this as the by-design funnel. If a purely mechanical attacker-input->execute() criterion were applied, this family would be a data-flow TP; the vulnerability-level verdict here is FP (by-design).

binding_or_barrier_evidence: base.py:1399-1403: SQLAlchemy 1.4.36 IdentifierPreparer.quote() — values requiring quotes are wrapped in dialect quotes AND embedded quote characters are escaped (IdentifierPreparer._escape_identifier: value.replace(escape_quote, escape_to_quote), e.g. " -> "" for the default preparer, backtick-escaped for MySQL). Values that do not require quotes are legal identifiers and cannot carry SQL syntax. This is effective identifier escaping, contrary to query_generation_notes.md §1 MySanitizers, which asserts quoting 'wrap[s] identifiers without escaping embedded quote characters'.

No server-side execution of the constructed statement: base.py:1415 database.compile_sqla_query(qry) (models/core.py:627-635, compile with literal_binds) and the SQL string is RETURNED to the client in the JSON response (api.py:854-861 result -> response; utils.py:92-99 payload['selectStar']). Executing it later requires the user to go through SQL Lab with its own access validation.

base.py:1395 database.get_columns(table_name, schema) (executed for show_cols/latest_partition) goes through the SQLAlchemy inspector, whose information_schema reflection queries bind table/schema as parameters.
Entry gated by can_access_table for the exact parsed table (decorators.py:54-66).
alerts.rationale: The sink is a definition-side fragment parameter, not an execution site; the downstream identifier is properly dialect-quoted/escaped, the compiled SELECT is returned as text rather than executed server-side, and the entry requires authenticated access to the exact table being named. No demonstrated injection.

provided_vulnerability_hit_analysis.vulnerability: CWE-89 SQL injection via the where_in Jinja macro (apache/superset commit 1d403dab9822a8cee6108669c53e53fad881c751, fix 'DB-specific quoting in Jinja macro (#25779)')

locations: superset/jinja_context.py:400-416 — where_in(values, mark="'"): inner quote() only doubles the *caller-chosen* mark character (value.replace(mark, mark*2), f"{mark}{value}{mark}"); a template author can pass an arbitrary mark, and values containing any other quote character (or non-string values via str(value)) are not escaped for the target dialect
superset/jinja_context.py:452 — self._env.filters["where_in"] = where_in (the pre-fix global-function registration; the fix replaces it with WhereInMacro(database.get_dialect()))

evidence: None of the 10 formal results is located in superset/jinja_context.py, references where_in, or tracks the values/mark arguments of the macro; all 10 alerts belong to the SQL Lab funnel and the select_star identifier flow.

The injection construction (f"{mark}{value}{mark}" / ", ".join, jinja_context.py:412-416) happens inside Jinja template rendering: jinja2 is external to the CodeQL database, so the filter call and its arguments never appear as Python data-flow nodes; only the whole rendered SQL string is propagated (MySummaries templateRenderFlow, jinja_context.py:458-469).

The attacker-reachable route that makes where_in a real vulnerability — chart viewers' filter values (request form_data -> filter_values()/get_filters() macros, jinja_context.py:487-488) rendered into a stored virtual-dataset template — has no modeled source path: the chart-data flow is broken at ChartDataQueryContextSchema().load (query_generation_notes.md §4, marshmallow external) and stored dataset SQL is second-order with no source (p5-none-050).

The SQL Lab route (a user writing {{ where_in(...) }} in the query editor) is covered by the funnel alerts only in the trivial whole-SQL-text sense (results #2/#5/#6/#7/#8/#9), which reflects by-design execution of the user's own query and does not demonstrate the quote-escaping flaw; the funnel alerts are themselves triaged FP above.
provided_vulnerability_hit_analysis.conclusion: The Pass 5 formal analysis did NOT hit the real where_in SQL injection vulnerability. The root causes are (a) the vulnerable escaping happens inside the external Jinja rendering engine at argument granularity the model does not track, and (b) the attacker-controlled route to those arguments (chart filter values into stored dataset templates) is explicitly out of the model's source scope. To capture this class, a future pass would need a source at the chart-data filter values, an edge through BaseTemplateProcessor filter calls, and a sink at the where_in construction (jinja_context.py:412/416), plus a barrier modeling the fixed WhereInMacro(dialect) quoting.

conclusion: CodeQL analysis succeeded and the 10 formal CWE-89 taint paths are all mechanically consistent with the real code, but none of them represents a genuine SQL injection vulnerability: 6 restatements of the by-design SQL Lab execute/estimate/validate funnel (authenticated, access-validated, user-authored whole statements) and 4 restatements of the select_star identifier flow (dialect-quoted, returned-not-executed, table-access-gated). 0 likely_tp / 10 likely_fp / 0 uncertain. The independently-provided real vulnerability of this snapshot (where_in Jinja macro quoting, fixed by commit 1d403dab) was not hit by the formal results.
